A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GmNet work, with matching architecture and principal experiments. All supplied pages are readable. v2 refers to supplementary material but ends with a checklist; v3 includes a technical appendix. Appendix additions are assessed as newly documented content, without assuming when the experiments were conducted.

before.justification: v2 reports original frequency-filtered classification experiments, ImageNet results, activation and GLU ablations, and convolution-kernel bandwidth analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and reports additional component ablations, spectral measurements, robustness tests, and downstream evaluations.

M1.justification: The proposed GmNet retains the ReLU6(x)·x gate, two 7×7 depth-wise convolutions, two pointwise convolutions, and the same model configurations. New pseudocode documents the existing design; alternative gates and ConvNeXt experiments do not establish a revision to GmNet.

E1.justification: v3 documents CUB-100 classification, MSCOCO 2017 object detection and instance segmentation, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and a CIFAR-10 adversarial testing scenario. v2 mentions downstream tasks but supplies no corresponding datasets or results. Existing frequency-filtered classification coverage is retained, including EfficientFormer experiments moved to the appendix.

E2.justification: The principal ImageNet comparator table is unchanged. v3 extends gate comparisons with FC-branch designs, SiLU and SwiGLU, and adds a ConvNeXt control comparison (Tables 4, 9, 11 and 13). EdgeViT and GhostNet are not new comparators: both already appear in v2 Figure 6.

E3.justification: v3 adds component comparisons controlling parameters and approximately matching FLOPs, layer-wise spectral-energy measurements using a central-quarter low-frequency region, optimizer-variation experiments using Adam at 0.001, and PGD testing. The existing ImageNet resolution, 300-epoch budget, AdamW optimizer, learning rate and batch size remain unchanged; newly disclosed recipes are documentation additions.

E4.justification: v3 adds component-attribution controls, FC and SiLU/SwiGLU gate ablations, activation replacement across model sizes, PGD robustness testing, quantitative spectra before and after gates, and optimizer sensitivity analyses. These test attribution, mechanisms and failure conditions beyond v2's activation, gate-design and kernel-bandwidth studies. Relocated threshold plots are retained analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run averages for frequency-learning experiments and five testings for selected ablations. v3 additionally reports mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds for the component breakdown in Table 5. It does not establish increased repetition of existing experiments.

E6.justification: The main ImageNet table and existing activation results remain unchanged, including GmNet-S3 at 79.3%. v3 adds substantial results: GmNet-S1 reaches 81.5% on CUB-100, ConvNeXt without/with GLU scores 82.5%/83.0%, and Table 15 reports 42.2 box AP, 40.1 mask AP and 44.6 mIoU for GmNet-S3. Additional ablation, spectral and robustness outcomes are newly reported results, not improvements over matched v2 experiments.

T1.justification: v3 removes the explicit integration-by-parts proof of v2 Theorem 2 while retaining the differentiation identity and smoothness–spectral-decay argument in informal form. It adds a discontinuity-decay example. The convolution theorem and spectrum-broadening argument remain substantively unchanged.

C1.justification: The core contributions remain frequency analysis of gating and the lightweight GmNet architecture. v3 explicitly claims the first systematic frequency analysis and strengthens the performance claim from competitive results to a new state of the art. Its introduction also asserts selective amplification of useful high-frequency signals while remaining robust to noise.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving shared gating representations, depth-dependent clipping effects, low-resolution limitations and the high-frequency/adversarial-robustness tradeoff. v2's standalone limitations section disappears, but its qualification about smaller benefits in larger architectures reappears with ConvNeXt evidence in Appendix A.8. These substantially expand the interpretation beyond the retained activation and bandwidth discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 supplies block pseudocode and detailed ResNet/GmNet training recipes, including normalization, layer scaling, regularization, augmentation and optimizer settings previously absent from the supplied v2. The model-configuration table is relocated unchanged. v3 also provides a code repository URL instead of v2's promise of release upon acceptance.

R1.justification: v3 removes background references including LSTM/GRU, the original Transformer, Focal Modulation and GELU, while retaining the central frequency-learning and lightweight-network literature. It more explicitly positions shared-representation gating against StarNet/EfficientMod designs and asserts an unfilled frequency-analysis gap.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and theoretical exposition are extensively rewritten around spectral bias in lightweight vision models. v3 reorganizes the closing sections, replaces the NeurIPS checklist with statements, introduces a structured technical appendix, and adopts conference headers and author–year citations.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the introductory example and ResNet block diagram, separates frequency curves into clearer panels, relocates retained threshold plots and model configurations, rescales the latency plot, and recolors the bandwidth histograms. New algorithm displays, ablation tables and appendix figures substantially change the visual organization.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves reproducibility through explicit pseudocode and training recipes, and strengthens the central design argument with component controls and direct spectral measurements absent from the supplied v2. Robustness and transfer experiments also make applicability more assessable. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, although PGD settings remain unspecified, some spectral interpretations overgeneralize Table 14, and the introduction's 81.3% GmNet-S3 claim conflicts with Table 1's unchanged 79.3%.
